Crowding and Chronic
journals.sagepub.com/home/eab
Physiological Stress
Among Children
Kimberly A. Rollings1 and Gary W. Evans2
Abstract
Chronic crowding within housing adversely affects psychological well-
being, yet little is known about how design attributes contribute to these
effects, especially among children. This cross-sectional study first examined
associations between residential interior density and children’s (M = 9
years of age) perceived bedroom and home crowding. Second, analyses
investigated whether interior design attributes (residential floor plan
arrangement measured by space syntax [depth and permeability]; bedroom
ceiling height, volume, and window area) buffer negative effects of perceived
crowding on multimethodological indices of child development, including
psychological distress, learned helplessness, and physiological stress. After
adjusting for home type, clutter, income, gender, and age, interior density
was significantly associated with perceived home and bedroom crowding.
Regression results suggested that bedroom ceiling height was associated with
reduced negative effects of home, but not bedroom, perceived crowding
on blood pressure, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and allostatic load among
participants who reported higher levels of perceived crowding.

Keywords
crowding, interior design, children, psychological health, physiological stress,
space syntax
Introduction
Research demonstrates that chronic crowding experienced within a high inte-
rior density residence negatively affects psychological health and physiologi-
cal stress (see reviews: Evans, 2003a, 2006; Leventhal & Newman, 2010).
Young children, especially those not in day care, spend more time at home
than in any other environment (Hofferth & Sandberg, 2004), yet few studies
have examined whether design attributes within a home buffer negative effects
of crowding on children (Evans, Lepore, & Schroeder, 1996; Schiffenbauer,
Brown, Perry, Shulack, & Zanzola, 1977). Considering increasing rates of
high-density living and emerging “tiny house” options, understanding how
interior design attributes affect the crowding–health relation is critical to
informing housing policy, especially for affordable housing. This cross-sec-
tional study first examined associations between residential interior density
(people per room) and children’s perceived crowding. We then examined
whether interior design elements such as floor plan arrangement and bedroom
ceiling height, volume, and window area moderated the effects of perceived
crowding on multimethodological indices of child development, including
psychological health and physiological stress.
Residential Interior Density and Crowding Defined
Density has been defined in a number of ways and at multiple scales, from
rooms and buildings to neighborhoods and cities. In the planning field, the
term “density” refers to neighborhoods and cities (i.e., number of people per
acre), while “crowding” refers to the density of interior spaces (Forsyth,
Oakes, Schmitz, & Hearst, 2007). In this article, however, the term residential
interior density indicates the number of persons per room within a home.
Crowding (noted as perceived crowding in the remainder of this article),
therefore, is defined as a psychological response to residential interior density
based on perceptions of spatial restriction due to too little space or too many
people present in a space (Aiello, Epstein, & Karlin, 1974; Evans, Saegert, &
Harris, 2001; Stokols, 1972a; Sundstrom, 1975). The number of residents per
room, rather than square footage per person, is a measure of density that is
more robustly associated with behavioral outcomes (Baum & Paulus, 1987;
Evans, 2006). Among the psychosocial processes leading from high density to
perceived crowding are diminished feelings of control, especially over desired

592 Environment and Behavior 51(5)
social interaction (Altman, 1975); overarousal or overstimulation (Evans,
1979); interference with goals and activities (Lepore, Evans, & Palsane, 1991;
Olson, 1975; Schiffenbauer et al., 1977); or interference with socially support-
ive relationships among home residents, leading to social withdrawal (Evans,
2003a). The following sections discuss (a) the effects of residential interior
density and crowding on children’s psychological health and physiological
stress and (b) previous research on design characteristics (e.g., floor plan con-
figuration) that may moderate the impacts of high interior density and per-
ceived crowding on human health and behavior.
Adverse Effects of Crowding, Measured by Interior Density
Many cross-sectional studies (Baum, Gatchel, Aiello, & Thompson, 1981;
Baum & Valins, 1979; Evans, 2003a; Evans & Lepore, 1993; Evans et al.,
1996; Evans, Palsane, Lepore, & Martin, 1989; Evans, Rhee, Forbes, Allen, &
Lepore, 2000; Evans et al., 2001; Lepore et al., 1991) and two prospective,
longitudinal studies (Lepore et al., 1991; Wells & Harris, 2007) found adverse
effects of chronic high interior density—an indicator of crowding—on adults’
psychological health. Although a substantial portion of the crowding literature
focuses on adults, several studies (see reviews: Evans, 1979, 2006; Leventhal
& Newman, 2010) examined interior density and children’s academic perfor-
mance, cognitive processes, psychological distress, helplessness, and chronic
stress. Earlier work on interior density and children controlled for socioeco-
nomic status (SES), but did not use standardized instruments to assess chil-
dren’s psychological health. Despite this limitation, results indicated that
children from higher interior density homes had more behavioral problems in
the classroom (Saegert, 1982). Greater conflict also occurred among parents
and children in higher interior density homes (Booth & Edwards, 1976; Evans,
Lepore, Sejwal, & Palsane, 1998; Saegert, 1982). High interior density further
affects children’s psychological health and development indirectly via effects
on parents’ behaviors. Parents in higher interior density homes tend to be more
critical and less responsive to their young children (Bradley & Caldwell, 1984;
Evans, Maxwell, & Hart, 1999; Wachs, 1989).
One study that did use a standardized index of psychological health found
significant associations between interior density and psychological health
among low-income children (Evans et al., 2001). Poor housing quality, includ-
ing high interior density, is a major source of stress and worry, especially for
low-income families (Evans, 2004; Evans, Lercher, & Kofler, 2002). Children
living in higher interior density conditions are more susceptible to learned
helplessness, likely because of greater difficulty in regulating social interac-
tions (Evans et al., 1998; Evans et al., 2002; Evans et al., 2001; Rodin, 1976).

Rollings and Evans 593
The relation between interior density and associated negative outcomes
may vary by gender, although the direction and presence of gender effects are
inconsistent. In the Evans and colleagues (2001) study, child participants from
higher interior density, multiple family dwellings were less likely to persist on
problem-solving tasks, but rural boys were more vulnerable to the adverse
psychological outcomes of high interior density than were girls. Another study
found that the association between interior density and learned helplessness
was significant only for 10- to 12-year-old girls (Evans et al., 1998).
Only a few studies have explored the effects of crowding on children’s
physiological stress outcomes (see review: Evans, 2006). A laboratory study
found that boys, but not girls, in high interior density conditions had higher
skin conductance levels; levels were even more elevated with longer expo-
sure (Aiello, Nicosia, & Thompson, 1979). Skin conductance, or electroder-
mal response, measures the skin’s response to physiological arousal from
internal or external stimuli. Another study found that 8- to 10-year-old boys
and girls from higher interior density apartments, especially with greater
family turmoil, had elevated overnight epinephrine and norepinephrine levels
(Evans & Saegert, 2000). In an additional study of 10- to 12-year-olds, gen-
der moderated the interior density–blood pressure relation such that increases
in interior density were significantly associated with increases in blood pres-
sure among boys when controlling for household income (Evans et al., 1998).
Several interior density studies focused on children examined gender as a
moderator, controlled for SES, and utilized standardized instruments to assess
children’s psychological health; not all studies, however, included a wide
range of residential interior densities (Evans, 2003a) or examined potential
moderators that might buffer the adverse effects of interior density on chil-
dren. Some evidence suggests that, conceivably, physical design elements
within a residence may moderate negative effects of interior density and per-
ceived crowding. This evidence is discussed in the following sections.
Interior Density, Perceived Crowding, and Residential Design
Elements: Potential Moderators
Policies focused explicitly on limiting interior density to avoid crowded liv-
ing conditions neglect potential design moderators of the density–crowding
relation. Schiffenbauer and colleagues (1977) concluded that “significant
variation in [perceived] crowdedness ratings with no variation in physical
(interior) density indicated that (interior) density is neither a necessary nor
sufficient condition for [perceived] crowding to occur” (p. 13). Schiffenbauer’s
team (1977) studied dormitory rooms of equal size and comparable number
of people per room, noting that perceptions of crowding differed based on

594 Environment and Behavior 51(5)
usable space, greater window vistas afforded by higher floor level, and
amount of natural light. Reduced usable space increased perceptions of
crowding, possibly because it elicited a lack of control over room layouts that
may have afforded additional privacy. Window views from higher floor lev-
els and more natural light, conversely, reduced perceptions of crowding.
Although this study suggested that residential design attributes may moderate
the interior density–perceived crowding relation, results were based on self-
reports from all female college students and did not consider alternative
explanations for differences in crowding perceptions. These findings were
replicated and expanded upon by Kaya and Erkip (2001), who found that
both male and female dormitory residents perceived rooms of equal size and
interior density on higher floor levels as less crowded than those on lower
floor levels. Evans et al. (2002) examined the effects of interior density and
dwelling type on self-reports and teacher reports of psychological distress.
They found that children living in multiple family dwellings with higher inte-
rior density, independently of SES, suffered greater psychological stress
compared with those in lower interior density dwellings, higher interior den-
sity single-family homes, and higher interior density row houses. In addition
to physical size, usable space, floor level, and natural light, additional
research offers evidence that design elements such as residential floor plan
arrangement, window area, and ceiling height could buffer the adverse effects
of interior density on children.
Floor plan arrangement and space syntax. Human needs to regulate social
interaction suggest that, given the same square footage, reactions to interior
density might vary based on floor plan arrangement (Aiello et al., 1974; Alt-
man, 1975; Evans et al., 1996; Stokols, 1972b; Sundstrom, 1975). Several
studies have linked floor plan arrangement to reduced perceptions of crowd-
ing among college students. A dormitory containing long corridors that was
converted into suite arrangements resulted in reduced negative outcomes of
perceived crowding, more social engagement, and less social withdrawal
(Baum & Davis, 1980). Other studies found that prison inmates experienced
lower levels of reported perceived crowding and less physiological stress in
cubicles compared with those housed in open floor plan arrangements, both
with a similar amount of square footage. This appeared to have occurred
because of enhanced opportunities to regulate social interaction in the cubi-
cles (Cox, Paulus, McCain, & Karlovac, 1982; Schaeffer, Baum, Paulus, &
Gaes, 1988).
Variations in floor plan configurations in the above illustrative studies can
be more formally quantified by space syntax. Space syntax describes how
attributes of residential floor plan layouts, such as depth and permeability,

can influence social interaction (Hillier & Hanson, 1984). Depth is defined as
the number of spaces or thresholds that must be traversed before reaching a
specific destination within a floor plan. Increased depth could afford desired
levels of privacy and social interaction, reducing social withdrawal (Evans
et al., 2000; Lepore, Merritt, Kawasaki, & Mancuso, 1990; Wells & Harris,
2007). While depth is a measure that describes floor plan layout, permeability
relates more to connectivity and openness. Permeability also describes how
floor plan layouts affect movement throughout a home (Hillier & Hanson,
1984). Permeability captures the accessibility of spaces and floor plan con-
figurations, or how public and private they are, and can be quantified by the
space syntax concepts of relative asymmetry (RA) and real relative asym-
metry (RRA; Hanson, 2003). RA is a function of the plan’s mean depth and
number of rooms, and RRA is a function of RA and depth of interconnected
spaces. Low values indicate highly public, integrated, and accessible spaces
and plan configurations, whereas high values indicate more private spaces
and plan configurations. Permeability also affords or inhibits control of stim-
ulation and social interaction that can affect perceptions of crowding (Hillier
& Hanson, 1984). An example floor plan and associated depth diagram are
presented in Figure 1.
In a promising study on residential environments concerning floor plan
arrangement and interior density, space syntax theory’s concept of architec-
tural depth was explored as a moderator of the interior density–psychological
distress relation in college students (Evans et al., 1996). The study found that
greater architectural depth moderated the interior density–psychological dis-
tress relation through added opportunities to regulate social interaction and

596 Environment and Behavior 51(5)
reduced social withdrawal (mediated moderator); therefore, negative effects
of high interior density on psychological distress were reduced. This density
by depth moderation matches findings that children living in higher interior
density homes who can retreat to a space of their own suffer fewer negative
effects of interior density (Wachs & Gruen, 1982).
Child’s bedroom ceiling height and window area. Although space syntax pro-
vides useful methods to quantify differences in two-dimensional floor plan
arrangements, the theory does not capture three-dimensional design ele-
ments, such as ceiling height or window area, that may affect perceptions of
room size and thus potentially moderate the impacts of interior density on
both perceived crowding and affective and physiological reactions to per-
ceived crowding.
Ceiling height and volume. Adults perceive rooms with lower ceilings as
smaller, offering less physical space, and therefore require more personal
space; however, a room of the same size with a higher ceiling is perceived as
larger and offering more personal space, so adults require less personal space
and are willing to tolerate more social interaction (Savinar, 1975). Although
no prior research examining effects of volume on perception of personal
space or crowding was identified, volume was included in this study’s analy-
ses. Volume relates to proportions of interior space and is relevant to interior
design and architectural practice.
Windows. Evidence from a few studies has suggested that natural light and
views provided by windows, affected by window size, can influence percep-
tions of both room size and crowding (Butler & Steuerwald, 1991; Ne’eman &
Hopkinson, 1970; Schiffenbauer et al., 1977). Any window view is preferred
over no view (Collins, 1975), and expanded window views afforded by higher
floor level were found to reduce perceptions of crowding (Schiffenbauer et al.,
1977) and result in higher restorative quality ratings (Masoudinejad & Hartig,
2018). College students perceived dormitory rooms that received more natural
light as less crowded than darker rooms (Baum & Davis, 1976; Schiffenbauer
et al., 1977). Dormitory studies, however, did not account for window size.
Other studies have also examined the effect of room size, natural light, and
window view on window size preferences. In smaller rooms, a larger window
in proportion to the wall was preferred (Butler & Steuerwald, 1991). Consider-
ing the lack of literature examining connections between interior density and
children’s perceived crowding, as well as the potential for design attributes to
buffer negative effects of children’s perceived crowding on indices of child
development, the following exploratory study was conducted.

Current Study: Research Aims
The present study had two aims. Aim 1 examined whether residential interior
density was, in fact, a significant indicator of children’s perceived home and
bedroom crowding among the study sample. Although interior density is
often used as a proxy for perceived crowding (Baum & Paulus, 1987; Evans
et al., 2001), prior work indicates that interior density may not be necessary
or sufficient for perceived crowding to occur (Schiffenbauer et al., 1977;
Stokols, 1972b). Few studies have empirically tested associations between
residential interior density and perceived crowding among children. Whether
and to what degree children perceive crowding and are affected by those
perceptions are understudied. Initial analyses explored the hypothesis that
higher residential interior densities are strongly correlated with and predict
children’s perceived home and bedroom crowding (Figure 2a). If the density–
perceived crowding association is weak among children, policies attempting
to minimize negative effects of perceived crowding may need to address fac-
tors in addition to residential interior density, such as interior design quality.
Aim 2 then explored the potential of design elements to moderate chil-
dren’s psychological health and chronic physiological stress outcomes related
to perceived crowding. Research about how residential design attributes buf-
fer adverse effects of perceived crowding among children is sparse.
Conceivably, design attributes that may affect social interaction within a
home, as well as perceptions of space, could moderate children’s responses to
high residential interior density. Exploratory Aim 2 analyses assessed whether
the perceived crowding–psychological health and perceived crowding–phys-
iological stress relations among children were moderated by floor plan
arrangement (depth and permeability) and the focus child’s bedroom (FCB)
window area, ceiling height (lowest point), and volume (Figure 2b). The
hypothesis was that greater FCB depth, window area, ceiling height, and vol-
ume would moderate negative effects of perceived FCB crowding, and that

598 Environment and Behavior 51(5)
mean home depth and permeability would buffer the negative effects of per-
ceived home crowding.
Method
Research Design and Participants
Secondary, cross-sectional data were extracted from the first wave of a longi-
tudinal data set (Wave 1, 1995-1999; mean age = 9 years). Home interviews
with 341 low- and middle-income children and their mothers were originally
conducted during two home visits by trained research assistants following a
uniform protocol (Evans, 2003b). Data were gathered on housing quality,
psychological health, physiological stress, and demographics of one “focus
child” and the child’s mother. The majority of participants (88%) were White
and resided in primarily rural areas throughout upstate New York. Fifty per-
cent of participants resided in detached, single-family homes; others resided
in duplexes, trailers, or multifamily residences (e.g., apartment buildings
between one and four stories). Trained research assistants also sketched par-
ticipants’ home floor plans and recorded information about children’s bed-
room design for a subset of 181 children. Floor plans, bedroom design
information, and outcome data for this subset of 181 children were analyzed
in the current study.
Constructs and Measures
Residential interior density is defined, for the purposes of this study, as the
number of persons per room within a home. Perceived crowding is defined as
an individual’s perceptions of spatial restriction due to too little space or too
many people present in a space. The nine-item, 3-point perceived crowding
scale used in this study (Online Appendix A) was modeled on a reliable and
valid index of adults’ perceived crowding, developed by Evans and col-
leagues (2000), that is sensitive to both field and laboratory levels of interior
density. Perceived crowding scale items were developed via an iterative pro-
cess with a separate sample of children—of similar age to children in this
study’s sample—that included ascertaining whether or not children under-
stood each scale item. The process included repeating children’s answers
back to them and then asking what they meant when they provided their
answer. A subset of items with high levels of inconsistency between the rat-
ing and the explanation were dropped from the scale. The scale has adequate
internal consistency (α = .72). Scale validity is indicated by its correlation
with residential density (r = −.35) and the fact that the perceived crowding

Rollings and Evans 599
items load on a separate principal components factor when run in a cluster
with items measuring stress and psychological health.
Additional predictors, covariates, and outcome variables are described in
Table 1. Home type (four categories) and clutter were included in regression
models to account for potential design differences between home types, such
as amount of available space, number and types of available spaces, noise
from adjacent units, ceiling height, and clutter, that could conceivably affect
a child’s perception of crowding and the perceived crowding–design attribute
interactions. Income-to-needs ratio, age, and gender were also included as
demographic covariates. Results were adjusted for SES as in previous litera-
ture. Because the age of participants ranged from 6 to 12 years in this study,
age was also included in regression models to account for differences in body
size, developmental stage, and potentially higher rates of room sharing
among younger versus older children. In addition, gender was included as a
covariate for three reasons. Although previous literature documents an incon-
sistent pattern of how the effects of perceived crowding and high interior
density might vary by gender, responses to high interior density could vary
based on differences in gender roles and expectations within the home. Boys
who spend more time outdoors than girls may also be affected by interior
density differently (Cleland et al., 2010). Furthermore, physiological out-
comes can vary by gender (e.g., body mass index [BMI] used to calculate
allostatic load). The following sections describe the dependent variables that
measured psychological health and chronic physiological stress.
Psychological health outcomes. Children’s psychological health was operation-
alized using three age-appropriate measures gathered by trained researchers
during “Wave 1” of the larger longitudinal study. First, the Rutter Children’s
Behavior Questionnaire (Cronbach’s α = .83; Boyle & Jones, 1985; Rutter,
Tizard, & Whitmore, 1970), a widely used standardized instrument with
well-documented psychometric properties, measures psychological health in
nonclinical samples of young children (Boyle & Jones, 1985; Evans et al.,
2001; Rutter et al., 1970). The child’s mother rated the 26 items on a 3-point
scale (0 = does not apply, 1 = applies somewhat, 2 = certainly applies) that
related to childhood symptoms of anxiety, depression (e.g., “often worries,
worried about many things”), and behavioral conduct disorders (e.g., “bullies
other children”). Higher scores indicated worse behavior associated with
poorer psychological health.
Second, psychological well-being was assessed via the Harter global self-
worth subscale. Children’s self-perception of psychological well-being was
indexed using the global self-worth subscale of the perceived competence

scale (Cronbach’s α = .67; Harter, 1982). This six-item subscale required
that children complete forced-choice format items, selecting which of two
opposite behavioral descriptions were “really true or sort of true of you.”
Sample items included the following: “Some kids like the kind of person they
are” versus “other kids often wish they were someone else,” and “Some kids
are often unhappy with themselves” versus “other kids are pretty pleased
with themselves.” Higher scores indicate higher self-ratings of self-worth.
Third, learned helplessness, related to human motivation (Evans, 2001b),
was measured using an age-appropriate behavioral index that assessed persis-
tence on a challenging task. A standard behavioral protocol (Glass & Singer,
1972) was adopted for 9-year-olds (Cohen, Evans, Stokols, & Krantz, 1986).
The challenging task consisted of giving the focus children a puzzle in which
they had to “visit” each object (e.g., an animal) on the paper by tracing over
interconnecting lines without lifting the pencil or doubling back on any line.
Participants were given instructions, a practice round using an easy version
of the task, and then told to work on the challenging version until solved or
until they felt unable to do so. For ethical reasons, children were then given a
readily solvable version of the puzzle to ensure that all children solved a
puzzle. The index of helplessness was persistence (time in seconds) on the
first challenging puzzle. Longer length of time indicated longer persistence
associated with higher task motivation. Variations of this helplessness index
have been used in numerous laboratory and field studies and are sensitive to
both manipulations of stimulus controllability and degree of exposure to
chronic, uncontrollable stressors (Cohen, 1980; Evans & Stecker, 2004;
Peterson, Maier, & Selgiman, 1995).

602 Environment and Behavior 51(5)
Chronic physiological stress outcomes. High interior density and other environ-
mental stressors, such as noise, elevate physiological stress in children
(Evans, 2001a). Chronic physiological stress data were obtained using singu-
lar indices, as well as a composite index called allostatic load. Higher values
indicate increased physiological stress for all six of the following variables.
Blood pressure tracks chronic stress (Krantz & Falconer, 1995). Children’s
resting systolic and diastolic blood pressure was recorded by trained research-
ers using an automated monitor (Critikon Corp., Tampa, FL: Dinamap Model
1846SXP) as the child sat quietly and read for 25 min. After discarding the
initial measurement, six additional measurements were taken and averaged to
achieve maximum reliability (Kamarck et al., 1992). Children were restricted
from engaging in vigorous physical activity for 1 hr before these assessments.
Neuroendocrine measures (cortisol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine)
were calculated from 12-hr overnight (8:00 p.m.-8:00 a.m.) total urine sam-
ples, kept on ice with a preservative (metabisulfite), and picked up the
morning following the at-home interview. Four 10-mL samples were ran-
domly extracted, processed (samples for catecholamine analysis are acidi-
fied), and deep frozen at −80°C for subsequent biochemical assays.
Epinephrine and norepinephrine were assayed with high-pressure liquid
chromatography with electrochemical detection (Riggin & Kissinger, 1977)
and free cortisol with a radioimmune assay (Contreras, Hane, & Tyrrell,
1986). Creatine was assayed to provide a statistical control for differences
in body mass and incomplete urine voiding (Baum & Grunberg, 1995;
Grunberg & Singer, 1990; Tietz, 1976).
Allostatic load or “allostasis” refers to a dynamic, interactive set of physi-
ological systems of equilibrium maintenance with which the human body
continuously adjusts its normal operating range in response to physical and
social demands (Evans, 2003b; Ganzel, Morris, & Wethington, 2010;
McEwen, 1998; McEwen & Stellar, 1993; Seeman & McEwen, 1996;
Sterling & Eyer, 1988). The ongoing maintenance of internal equilibrium
increases allostatic load, which reflects chronic wear and tear on the body
caused by the mobilization of resources to meet environmental demands
(McEwen, 1998). An allostatic load index was created by summing dichoto-
mized (e.g., 1 = within the top quartile of risk, 0 = not within top quartile)
resting blood pressure (diastolic and systolic); overnight urinary neuroendo-
crine measures of cortisol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine; and BMI (Evans,
2003b; Kubzansky, Kawachi, & Sparrow, 1999; McEwen, 1998; Seeman,
McEwen, Rowe, & Singer, 2001; Seeman, Singer, Rowe, Horwitz, &
McEwen, 1997; Seeman, Singer, Ryff, Love, & Levy-Storms, 2002; Singer
& Ryff, 1999). BMI, an index of metabolic function, reflects body fat and
was calculated by dividing weight (kg) by squared height (m2). Evidence

Rollings and Evans 603
indicates that allostatic load is a better index of chronic stress than any singu-
lar component that constitutes this index (McEwen, 1998; Seeman et al.,
2001; Seeman et al., 1997).
Procedure
Interior density, perceived crowding, ceiling height, volume, floor plan
sketches, covariates, psychological health, and physiological stress measures
extracted from the original longitudinal data set were initially collected dur-
ing in-person interviews and observations conducted by pairs of trained
research assistants (Evans, 2003b). Participants were informed that the
study’s purpose was to explore housing and child well-being. Floor plan
sketches were used to calculate depth and permeability, according to Hillier
and Hanson’s (1984) procedures, by trained research assistants who had no
knowledge of participants’ residence or outcome measures.
Data analysis. IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows (IBM Corp., Version 24) was
used for statistical analyses. Pearson’s product–moment correlation coeffi-
cients were first calculated for FCB and home interior density, perceived FCB
and home crowding, FCB and home clutter, and home type (Aim 1). Regres-
sion models also examined interior density as a predictor of children’s per-
ceived home and bedroom crowding, accounting for home type, clutter,
income-to-needs, gender, and age (Aim 1). Then, regression models (Aim 2)
investigated the potential interactive effects of perceived crowding (home and
FCB) and each design attribute (home depth, home permeability, FCB depth,
FCB ceiling height, FCB window area, FCB volume) on the dependent vari-
ables. All regression models included home type, clutter, income-to-needs,
gender, and age. For comparison, regressions were also run with home and
FCB density—not perceived crowding—measures.
As little prior work has examined the potential for design attributes to
moderate effects of crowding on well-being, two measures were taken to
address the exploratory analytical approach to Aim 2. First, the error from
multiple significance testing, or running of many (54 total) statistical tests,
was corrected using a method called false discovery rate (FDR; Benjamini &
Hochberg, 1995; Benjamini & Yekutieli, 2001, 2005; Genovese, Lazar, &
Nichols, 2002; Yekutieli & Benjamini, 1999). Unlike Bonferroni corrections
that focus on controlling the probability of obtaining at least one false posi-
tive, FDR corrections have more power and control the proportion of falsely
rejected hypotheses within significant results. FDR procedures adjust origi-
nal p values and are reported as q values (Storey, 2003). In this study, the
q-value cutoff was set to .1, meaning that the probability of obtaining a false

604 Environment and Behavior 51(5)
positive was 10% and that 90% of the significant results were expected to be
true positive. A q value of .1, and not .05, was selected due to the relatively
small sample size and preliminary nature of this study; results below the .1
level suggest findings worthy of further investigation (Dahiru, 2008; Fisher,
1925, 1935; Gigerenzer, Krauss, & Vitouch, 2004). The R software (version
3.0.1) package “qvalues” was used to calculate corresponding q values
(Storey, Bass, Dabney, & Robinson, 2015) for two sets of Aim 2 analyses.
Second, two sets of analyses were run based on whether hypotheses related
to specific design attributes were a priori (based on previous literature) or
exploratory (little or no previous literature). One-sided tests were run for the
27 a priori hypotheses that included FCB ceiling height, window area, and
mean home depth as design attribute moderators. Resulting FDR q values
were divided by 2 to reflect the one-sided tests. The remaining 27 exploratory
tests examined FCB depth, FCB volume, and home permeability via two-
tailed tests.
Results
Participant sociodemographics and descriptive information about their home
environments are displayed in Table 2. Forty-two percent of participating
children shared a bedroom with at least one other person. Parents reported
that all participating children had a place to be alone, 81% of which were
separate, closed spaces that did not open onto other high activity spaces such
as kitchens or living areas. Only 19% of participants lived in multifamily
units and 14% in trailers. Fifty percent of families resided in detached, single-
family homes and another 17% in duplexes or row houses. With the excep-
tion of one four-story unit, all multifamily units were three stories or less.

perceived crowding (r = −.35, respectively). Home interior density was also
significantly correlated with perceived FCB crowding (r = −.27). FCB and
home interior density, as well as perceived crowding measures, were also
significantly positively correlated (r = .57 and r = .55, respectively). Clutter

Aim 2: Child Outcomes of Crowding
Table 5 and Figure 3a-e display the five a priori regression models (out of 27)
that contained significant interaction terms after FDR corrections for multi-

ceived home crowding and FCB ceiling height on physiological health
outcomes. Figure 3a-e illustrates the direction of these interactions, with
higher values indicating poorer outcomes. Continuous perceived crowding
and FCB ceiling height variables were dichotomized for illustrative purposes
only (Figure 3). All regression analyses maintained the original continuous
variables. Results indicated a significant main effect of FCB ceiling height
such that lower FCB ceiling heights were associated with poorer participant
physiological health outcomes, overall, when compared with outcomes of
participants with higher FCB ceiling heights. Results also suggested that
FCB ceiling height buffered the negative effects of perceived home crowding
on physiological stress outcomes, with the exception of cortisol, as antici-
pated. Higher FCB ceiling heights were associated with significantly lower
resting systolic (β = 0.80, q < .05; Figure 3a) and diastolic blood pressure (β

linkages between perceived home crowding and physiological health out-

Discussion
The purpose of this study was to (a) examine the relation between residential
interior density and children’s perceived crowding and (b) investigate the
potential of design attributes to buffer the adverse effects of perceived crowd-
ing on children’s psychological health and physiological stress. Aim 1 results
yielded consistent support for the hypothesis that higher residential interior
density is associated with greater perceived crowding both in the overall
home and for children’s bedrooms. Given that one of the primary contribu-
tors to perceived crowding is difficulties in regulating social interaction, the
significant associations between bedroom and household interior density and
perceived crowding make sense. Homes and bedrooms with higher interior
densities may make it more difficult for children to be away from people
when desired, and therefore they perceive crowding related to high density.
Although not a surprising finding, it is also worth noting that the child’s bed-
room interior density was significantly correlated with perceptions of not
only perceived bedroom crowding but also household crowding (Aim 1,
Table 3). The same pattern was uncovered for home interior density and per-
ceived bedroom and household crowding. These results suggest that interior
density of a child’s bedroom or home may be associated with perceived
crowding, and that both bedroom and home design attributes could poten-
tially serve as moderators of the negative effects of crowding.
Five a priori Aim 2 models indicated that higher FCB ceiling heights were
associated with attenuated linkages between perceived home crowding and
several markers of chronic physiological stress, especially among more
crowded participants. Prior work examining effects of ceiling height on adults’
personal space perceptions offers a possible explanation for the potential mod-
erating effect of ceiling height found in the present study. Adults in rooms with
a higher ceiling perceived having more personal space when compared with
adults in rooms of the same size with a lower ceiling height (Savinar, 1975).
In the present study, child participants in bedrooms with higher verses lower
ceilings may have, similarly, perceived greater amounts of personal space and
thus experienced attenuated effects of perceived crowding. Another possible

Rollings and Evans 611
explanation is that higher ceilings increased perceived volume or overall room
size, in turn reducing perceived crowding. Higher ceilings could also be asso-
ciated with bedroom space use, such as the inclusion of bunkbeds that increase
available floor space and lower perceptions of crowding. Future work can
pursue each of these possible models for why ceiling height might affect per-
ceived crowding. The first explanation can be explored by assessing the size
and shape of children’s personal space bubbles; the second can be explored via
a standardized psychophysical technique, such as magnitude estimation, to
document perceptions of room size. Study results also expanded upon find-
ings that suggest children living in high interior density homes who can retreat
to a space of their own, such as a bedroom, suffer fewer negative effects of
high interior density (Wachs & Gruen, 1982). Children who perceive having
more control over social interactions and the ability to control the number of
people in their space by retreating to a bedroom may have experienced attenu-
ated effects of high interior density and perceived crowding in this study
(Altman, 1975; Evans et al., 2001; Rodin, 1976). Design attributes of the bed-
room, including ceiling height based on study results, may also play a role.
The Aim 2 methodological approach consisted of running 54 statistical
tests and yielded only five significant results after FDR corrections, so results
of this exploratory work should be interpreted with caution. However, ceiling
height moderated effects of perceived crowding on five of the six physiologi-
cal stress outcomes examined, as expected, and 90% or 4.5 of the five signifi-
cant results are expected to be “true positive” based on FDR corrections.
More generally, exploratory analysis is a critical first step in the early stages
of inquiry, particularly for questions that have seen little or no prior analysis
(Winkel, Saegert, & Evans, 2009). Results offer some insights to guide future
research on the potential for design attributes to attenuate negative effects of
perceived crowding on children’s well-being.
The lack of significant results on psychological well-being may be due, in
part, to greater sensitivity of physiological markers than self-reported mea-
sures. The divergence of findings for physiological and self-reported mea-
sures also serves as an important reminder that overreliance on self-reported
measures is a major impediment to scientific progress in environmental psy-
chology (Winkel et al., 2009). Furthermore, the lack of significant explor-
atory model results and significant moderation by other design attributes
(home permeability, mean home depth, and FCB window area, volume, and
depth) may have been partially due to the limited variability among design
attributes and a small sample size that precluded use of advanced statistical
models that simultaneously examine all design attributes. Additional work is
needed to explore how these design attributes contribute to perceived crowd-
ing and whether they affect psychological outcomes.

612 Environment and Behavior 51(5)
The study contributes to the crowding literature in four ways. First, few
studies have examined the potential of design attributes to moderate the
relations between perceived crowding and psychological well-being or
with physiological stress generally, and this is especially true for children.
The relation between interior density and perceived crowding may differ
among children when compared with adults. Residential interior density
alone may not be enough to induce adverse effects of perceived crowding
among child participants, as suggested by the modest correlations found in
this study. Other social stressors within and physical characteristics of the
home (e.g., parenting, acoustics, window height, window treatments, hous-
ing quality) may influence the interior density–perceived crowding relation
(Schiffenbauer et al., 1977; Stokols, 1972b). Furthermore, social interac-
tion and privacy may be regulated through both psychological and environ-
mental coping processes (Altman, 1975; Archea, 1977; Evans et al., 1996).
Second, standardized indices of children’s psychological health and physi-
ological stress were used. Most studies on crowding (via multiple mea-
sures) and children have not relied on standardized instruments to assess
mental health, and physiological stress outcomes are rare. Third, this study
is one of few that explored the predictive validity of depth and permeabil-
ity, two space syntax theoretical constructs.
Finally, this study provided evidence that FCB ceiling height has the
potential to buffer adverse effects of perceived home crowding, especially
among children reporting higher levels of perceived home crowding, and
positively affect children’s health and well-being. The potential for ceiling
height to attenuate the negative effects of perceived crowding is an especially
critical finding considering current and anticipated increases in residential
interior density, especially among low-income populations and in urban areas
where square footage is limited. Additional studies must explore whether the
potential well-being benefits of raising ceiling heights in high-density living
conditions outweigh increases in construction costs.
Limitations
Like much of the crowding literature, this study was cross-sectional and
concerns about causality are tantamount. Although models were adjusted
for income—and somewhat addressed self-selection as parents, not chil-
dren, select where they live—there are many plausible alternative explana-
tions that might explain the results of the study. Length of exposure to high
interior density in the home and bedroom, previous living conditions, par-
ent behavior and well-being, noise, and other stressors in and outside of the
home were also not considered in this study. At low levels of residential

Rollings and Evans 613
interior density, the relation between interior density, perceived crowding,
and negative outcomes likely depends upon other psychological, environ-
mental, and situational factors (Gillis, 1979). At higher levels of interior
density, the probability of experiencing adverse effects of perceived crowd-
ing increases, as well as other factors associated with high interior density
influencing discomfort.
Second, the association between housing design elements and children’s
well-being may vary by individual child characteristics (e.g., age) and over
time. For instance, the interactive effects of ceiling height and perceived
crowding may change over time as children age. Associations between per-
ceived crowding and well-being may be stronger for younger children who
spend more time inside the home when compared with adolescents (Leventhal
& Newman, 2010). Conversely, children’s growth in size as they age may
make a bedroom feel increasingly smaller. As children enter into adoles-
cence, however, they may be able to more easily escape the pressures of
unwanted social interaction by leaving the residence. A future longitudinal or
intervention study would help establish causality (Evans et al., 1996). Third,
the small sample size and low variability among study variables may also
partially explain the lack of significant results for design attributes other than
ceiling height. A wider and more representative range of residential interior
densities, housing design attributes (window area, ceiling height), and child
sociodemographic factors, in addition to a larger sample size, would
strengthen the study design and generalizability. A larger sample size would
also allow use of more advanced statistical models (e.g., structural equation
modeling) to simultaneously examine all design attributes and outcomes.
Multiple design attributes likely affect how density is perceived, so a simul-
taneous examination of multiple design attributes—rather than one-at-a-
time—is needed. The reliability of perceived crowding measures used with
young children also requires further testing. Additional interior design attri-
butes such as openness, visual access, acoustic treatments, and lighting may
also affect perceptions of residential interior density. Furthermore, study
results were inconsistent with prior work on depth. Mean home depth did not
moderate the interior density–psychological distress relation among children
as in prior studies of college students in off-campus housing (Evans et al.,
1996). Per parent reports, the child participants all had a place to be alone and
resided in low-rise buildings (4 stories or less) in rural areas and small towns.
Effects of design attributes, including depth, in taller buildings and urban
areas may differ. Additional work is needed to examine the effects of depth
and other design attributes on the perceived crowding–psychological health
relationship among young children.

614 Environment and Behavior 51(5)
Implications and Conclusions
Crowding is a widely acknowledged source of adult stress that detracts from
housing quality, yet little is known about the effects of crowding on children.
Study results suggest associations between interior density and perceived
crowding among children, and that ceiling height might moderate negative
effects of perceived crowding on children’s well-being. High interior den-
sity conditions negatively affect children’s well-being, including academic
achievement, behavior, health, SES, and adult well-being (Lopoo & London,
2016; Solari & Mare, 2012). Low-income populations facing multiple envi-
ronmental and psychological stressors are, furthermore, most likely to be
affected by high interior density and perceived crowding (Evans & English,
2002; Gillis, 1979; Saegert, 1982). Identifying design elements that enable
people to cope better with high interior densities, as well as other suboptimal
living conditions, is necessary to guide housing policy and accommodate
expected increases in high interior density living conditions (Mackun,
Wilson, Fischetti, & Goworowska, 2011). This knowledge can inform the
design, construction, and renovation of existing and future high interior den-
sity housing developments without introducing additional or worsening
existing housing stressors.
This study explored the potential of interior design attributes to modify
children’s responses to perceived crowding and offers directions for future
research. The study examined design as a potential moderator of perceived
crowding, an environmental phenomenon with well-documented effects
on human behavior. Results suggest that other physical design features,
beyond available floor space, may have some utility in attenuating the
negative effects of high interior density associated with crowding, typi-
cally measured by a lack of space or interference with desired levels of
social interaction. These additional design features may provide designers,
who often make claims about how design can affect perceptions of avail-
able space, with a richer evidence-based toolbox from which to address
high interior density.
Increasing residential ceiling heights or adjusting other design attributes
that affect perceptions of ceiling height, especially when increasing square
footage is not possible, could buffer adverse effects of perceived crowding on
residents, including children.
